challenge.top10_critique:
The ranking is weighted toward the wrong things. Six of the ten items are bookkeeping carried over from the peer's transactional runtime: resume-call-keys, variant-base-clean-apply, usage-ledger, orchestrator-sole-writer, done-amendment-record, and the hashing half of frozen-check-inputs. They protect budget and records, not whether the output is correct. They are also the rules an LLM orchestrator follows least reliably from prose, and together they need about 210 words that SKILL.md (995/1000) does not have.

Three of them rest on weak or misread evidence:
- The resume-keys root cause was added to the log in c3eebb2, after the fact.
- The `base` failure comes from v1-era winner carry-over, which v2 removed.
- The keep-oscillation 'regression' does not exist.

Meanwhile the one item that measures the loop's core instrument, seeded-defect-probe, is ranked #8 and tests only the pairwise side.

Proposed top 10:
1. seeded-defect-probe, extended to the Check. A miss turns on strict mode and tells the human.
2. verdict-error-class, with the apply check folded in and UNKNOWN kept separate from tie (missing item 1).
3. frozen-check-inputs. Tests and config the generator adds never count toward DONE, and checks run in a disposable copy.
4. judge-family-correlation.
5. recheck-unchanged-best.
6. output-status-labels.
7. orchestrator-sole-writer.
8. A deterministic checker script for hosts with a shell or a Workflow engine. It absorbs counts-from-records, the hashes and the archive lint.
9. done-amendment-record, with hashes computed by command.
10. Round-atomic resume: the reduced resume-call-keys plus judged-text-hash's write order.

usage-ledger drops to med (count rounds and time), and variant-base-clean-apply merges into #2. The net SKILL cost is about 120 words instead of 210, and less if the script takes over the bookkeeping. The ~115-word shortfall then mostly disappears without raising the cap.

A CS professor would name one change as most important: calibrate the instrument before adding rules to what it measures. Every keep, veto, Check pass and held-out majority assumes LLM judges notice regressions. The repo has no measurement of v2's false-acceptance or missed-defect rate. v2 has never run end-to-end (DESIGN 'Not yet proven'). Its entire validation was LLM agents reading the spec text (v2-validation.json, v2-revalidation.json), which is itself a preference measurement. Every 'measured' failure in this register comes from v1-era designs. The literature says leniency is the dominant error: in 2510.11822 (abstract verified), validators have a true-positive rate of 96% but a true-negative rate under 25%, and majority voting does not fix it.

So the change is: run v2 on a known-answer artifact with seeded defects plus a negative control. Record the false-acceptance and missed-defect rates of both the pairwise judges and the pass/fail Check. Compare against a matched-budget baseline that has the same Verifier and checks, using quality-versus-cost curves. Until that exists, every rule here, the ten above included, is effectively design-only, and adding more of them mostly enlarges what the unaudited orchestrator can misapply. Inside SKILL.md, the per-run version of that measurement is the seeded-defect probe on both judges and the Check, which is why it ranks #1.

papers.title: AgentDropout: Dynamic Agent Elimination for Token-Efficient and High-Performance LLM-Based Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.venue_year: ACL 2025: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 24013-24035, Vienna, July 2025. Authors: Zhexuan Wang, Yutong Wang, Xuebo Liu, Liang Ding, Miao Zhang, Jie Liu, Min Zhang
papers.how_verified: I opened the ACL Anthology page to check the title, authors, pages and DOI. I then downloaded the full ACL PDF, extracted its text with PyMuPDF and read the abstract, setup (4.1), main results, analysis, ablations and limitations myself. The WebFetch summary of the PDF made up three claims that are not in the PDF: a '40-50% token reduction', 'Claude-3', and 'beats a single agent at equal token budgets'.
papers.finding: It learns per-round communication-graph adjacency matrices from 40 training samples per benchmark, then drops low-degree agents (Node Dropout) and low-weight edges (Edge Dropout). Against AgentPrune it uses 21.6% fewer prompt tokens and 18.4% fewer completion tokens, with +1.14 average accuracy (Llama3-8B +2.19, Qwen2.5-72B +0.77, DeepSeek-V3 +0.47). Dropping nodes or edges at random lowers performance.
papers.relevance: Weak, indirect support for the loop's lean participation: one judge first, more only when unsure, and not every role in every round. The paper reports that using different roles in different rounds beats using the same roles every round. It says nothing about judge ensembles or majority votes, role independence, verification or termination.
papers.caveat: The tasks are short-answer QA, math and code benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, AQuA, MultiArith, SVAMP, HumanEval) run as a multi-round discussion system. The topology is trained on labeled data with a task utility. The RQGM loop has one artifact and no training set, so the method does not transfer; only the direction of the finding does. Gains are about 1 point. There is no matched-budget comparison against a single agent: token comparisons are against other multi-agent baselines, and SC(CoT) uses 5 samples.

Authors: Mert Cemri, Melissa Z Pan, Shuyi Yang, Lakshya A Agrawal, Bhavya Chopra, Rishabh Tiwari, Kurt Keutzer, Aditya Parameswaran, Dan Klein, Kannan Ramchandran, Matei A Zaharia, Joseph E Gonzalez, Ion Stoica
papers.how_verified: I opened the NeurIPS proceedings page, which confirms the title, authors, D&B track, DOI and abstract. I downloaded the full arXiv v3 HTML (2503.13657) and checked the failure-mode percentages, kappas and Table 5 intervention numbers in the raw text. The arXiv comments field does not mention NeurIPS; the proceedings page does.
papers.finding: MAST-Data has 1600+ traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks. It defines 14 failure modes in 3 categories: system design, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Human agreement is kappa 0.88; the o1 annotator reaches kappa 0.77 and 94% accuracy (0.79 out of domain). Verifiers often check only superficially. Adding a high-level objective verification step to ChatDev raised success from 25.0% to 40.6% on 32 tasks.
papers.relevance: Supports the loop's explicit HALT and termination rules and '[OPEN] blocks Stop': FM-1.5 'unaware of termination conditions' is 12.4% of failures and appears almost only in failed runs; FM-3.1 'premature termination' is 6.2%. Supports multi-level verification (Verifier + mechanical checks + DONE-criterion judges), since FM-3.2 no/incomplete verification is 8.2%, FM-3.3 incorrect verification is 9.1%, and 'Insight 3' says multi-level verification is needed. Supports the ledger against repeated ideas: FM-1.3 step repetition is 15.7%. It also offers a failure vocabulary the loop could use to tag its own run logs after the fact.
papers.caveat: This is a taxonomy and diagnostic dataset, not an evaluation of RQGM-style improvement loops. The intervention evidence is two small case studies. On ChatDev ProgramDev-v0 (n=32), +9.4 points is 3 tasks and +15.6 points is 5 tasks; AG2 on GSM-Plus gains about 1-5 points. All use the same model with no matched-budget control, and the authors call the gains not substantial. The percentages are shares of annotated failures, not per-run failure rates. The frameworks and models are older (ChatDev, MetaGPT, AG2, GPT-4/Claude 3 era).

Challenger evaluators co-evolve and replace the incumbent only if they statistically beat it on a held-out ground-truth anchor; ties keep the incumbent, and scores that depended on the old evaluator are erased. Supports the tie-to-incumbent keep rule, final scoring by fixed external judges not used in search, and matched-budget reporting: best at matched compute and cost to matched quality, with blended tokens where output counts 5x. It points to a mechanism the loop lacks, selective erasure: when the rung changes, verdicts and ledger rejections made under the old rubric should not carry over. It does NOT support majority voting: the text contains no majority or voting rule, and panel results are per-reviewer acceptance plus the panel mean. So DESIGN.md row 8's '[paper] RQGM: evolving evaluators' supports evolving and held-out evaluation, not the 'decided by majority' rule. The loop has no anchor and uses human decisions instead, so the paper's per-epoch guarantees do not transfer. Evaluators co-evolve in a codebase shared with the task agents, unlike the loop's isolated roles. One of the four panel reviewers is RQGM's own adversarial reviewer. Coding result: 71.7% vs 69.9% held-out pass rate, using 1.35-1.72x fewer tokens.

litA.notes:
I verified all five requested sources, plus one extra source the peer cites, against primary pages. I opened each page and checked the numbers in the raw text: extracted PDF or arXiv HTML, not WebFetch summaries. WebFetch's summaries were unreliable. For AgentDropout it invented a 40-50% token reduction, Claude-3, and a matched-budget win over a single agent. For 2607.27942 it reversed the loop-usage statistic. Use the numbers above, not a fresh WebFetch summary. Label all six entries 'literature'. None of them upgrades the peer's own design-only content (state machine, invariants I01-I20, verifier levels, ADRs). The peer's short summaries of these papers are accurate but thin.

Implications for the RQGM loop, each with its evidence label:
1. Correct an attribution in DESIGN.md row 8 (literature, RQGM 2606.26294 plus author blog). The RQGM paper never uses majority voting. It scores with one frozen evaluator per epoch and reports a fixed four-reviewer panel as per-reviewer rates plus the panel mean. It supports evolving evaluators, held-out external judges and ties keeping the incumbent, not 'decided by majority'. None of the five sources directly supports the held-out majority rule, so that rule stays design-only unless another source backs it.
2. Consider adding selective erasure at rung escalation (literature, RQGM). When the bar rises, ledger rejections and pairwise verdicts recorded under the old rubric should be dropped or re-judged, not reused. Mixing evidence from different utilities breaks the paper's per-epoch guarantee.
3. The matched-budget baseline is more urgent than DESIGN.md's 'Not yet proven' section suggests (literature, 2512.08296v3). At matched tokens, the mean multi-agent change was -0.3%, with a range from -70% to +81%. Adding agents gave negative returns once a single agent exceeded about 45% accuracy. The loop has no evidence that it beats a single agent or best-of-N at the same token spend.
4. Do not cite 2512.08296's 17.2x error amplification against independent judges. Its Independent arm concatenated outputs with no voting or cross-checking. The relevant finding is that a central validation bottleneck contained errors (4.4x), which fits the loop's one-orchestrator-plus-Verifier design.
5. Explicit termination rules and multi-level verification are supported (literature, MAST). Unaware-of-termination failures (12.4%) appear almost only in failed runs. Verifiers are often superficial, and adding a high-level objective check helped, though only by 5 tasks out of 32.
6. Checkers should be adversarial and enforced by the orchestrator, not optional for an agent, and results should be checked across runs (literature, 2607.27942). Downstream checkers ratified upstream framing, agent-optional loops mostly went unused, and fewer than half of solved tasks were solved in every run. The evidence is one benchmark with GPT-5-mini/nano only.
7. AgentDropout gives only weak directional support for not running every role every round. Its method needs labeled training data and does not transfer to one-artifact runs.

None of these sources tests an artifact-improvement loop with judges. All are task-solving multi-agent studies, a diagnostic taxonomy, or the RQGM preprint itself. I made no repo edits. litB.notes:
This was a read-only literature task: no repo or peer files were modified. For each of the 12 papers above I opened the arXiv abs page with WebFetch on 2026-09-25 and checked title, authors, date and venue. None of them is in runs/2026-09-22-meta/research.json. Every paper counts as "literature". How it applies to RQGM is design-only until a run measures it. I did not upgrade the peer (Codex) material, which stays design-only.

Answers by question (with the sources above):

Q1 (judge ensembles, correlated errors):
- The errors are correlated. It is worst within one provider or family, but strong models converge even across families (2506.07962).
- Measured same-family lift is 3.4-8.4 pp, and 55.4% of AB/BA pairs reverse (2609.17857).
- Judges are lenient: TPR 96% but TNR under 25%. A minority veto beats majority voting (2510.11822).
- Reference or known-answer anchors largely fix judge-competence limits (2503.05061).
- Measured mitigations: mixing families (2502.08788), both-order judging, minority veto, reference answers.
- Implication: the Check and held-out majorities are not independent votes. Consider a veto or strict rule at the final pass, and planted-defect canaries.

Q2 (loop vs. matched-compute baseline):
- At equal tokens, self-refine and reflexion lose to repeated sampling, but only in small-model math (2607.28576).
- Majority vote explains most debate gains (2508.17536).
- Debate often fails to beat CoT or Self-Consistency (2502.08788).
- Together with 2607.12227 (already in repo), this strengthens the case for a budget-matched baseline arm in RQGM validation: N fresh regenerations judged by the same held-out panel.

Q3 (multi-agent vs. single-agent):
- Architecture-task fit decides the outcome: +80.8% on decomposable tasks, -70.0% on sequential ones (2512.08296).
- Independence helps judging. Communication among homogeneous agents does not (2508.17536, 2502.08788).

Q4 (seeded defects):
- FLAWS (2511.21843): the best reviewer finds only 39.1% of planted errors, even at k=10.
- Mutation-oracle critic loop with a pre-registered causal estimate, plus a warning that a harness artifact produced a p=9.5e-66 false effect (2607.23002).

Q5 (budget and stopping):
- Same-task token use varies up to 30x, and models cannot self-predict it (r ≤ 0.39) (2604.22750).
- Cost-aware optimal stopping for refinement (2608.10729, CDC 2026).

Also verified (abs page opened) but left out to stay within the 12-paper cap:
- 2609.02246 'LLM-as-a-Judge Is Not an Oracle' (Wahi, Sep 2026): practitioner report. Its PROCTOR framework uses canary cases, frozen holdouts, acceptance checks that override the judge, and capability-disjoint roles. It reports a 100% pass rate that hid 68% true capability.
- 2604.19049 'Refute-or-Promote' (Agarwal, Apr 2026): single-author case study. Ten reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent padding oracle, and only an empirical gate caught it. About 79% of 171 candidates were killed.
- 2505.11855 SPOT (Son et al., May 2025): on real errata-level errors, no model exceeds 21.1% recall or 6.1% precision.
- 2607.12885 (Kranti and Vajjala, Jul 2026): without a reference, judges over-credit wrong answers; adding a reference changes up to 85% of decisions.
- 2511.17006 BATS (COLM 2026): an in-context budget tracker. A larger budget alone does not help without budget awareness.
- 2601.14470 Tokenomics (Jan 2026): in ChatDev, iterative review takes 59.4% of tokens and input tokens 53.9%.
- 2605.00914 'The Cost of Consensus' (Apr 2026): homogeneous debate spends 2.1-3.4x more tokens for equal or lower accuracy than isolated self-correction.
- 2606.01034 and 2608.19802 (Zhu, Xie, Rao; WISE 2026): judge-panel calibration and routing. The policy drops redundant 'copy' judges and stops when validation gain falls below a threshold.
- 2502.04313 'Great Models Think Alike' (Goel et al., 2025): the CAPA similarity metric; judges favour similar models.
- 2505.13778 CoIn: auditing hidden reasoning-token billing. Only tangentially relevant.
- Counter-evidence: 2608.05643 'Refining Over Resampling' (Aug 2026, submitted to EMNLP) reports refinement beating majority voting. Its abstract does not show a token-matched comparison, so it neither confirms nor refutes the Q2 finding.

Numbers I saw only in search snippets and not in the abstracts are excluded: the 17.2x/4.4x error amplification and ~45% saturation from 2512.08296, the kappa 0.47 to 0.85 from 2503.05061, and the MAD win rate below 20% from 2502.08788.

Gap: I found no published seeded-defect study of LLM judges accepting or rejecting whole prose artifacts in a pairwise improvement loop. The closest are FLAWS (paper error localization) and the mutation-testing paper (code only). The peer's V0-V4 PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN/ERROR verifier and known-answer anchors therefore remain design-only for RQGM.

rRuntime.notes:
I read all six slice files in full, plus SKILL.md, INITIATOR.md, DESIGN.md and every run record, and edited nothing. All peer content in this slice is design-only. Its reference.py implements only point-version checks in memory (CONTRACTS.md 'Reference-only simplifications'), so its passing tests say nothing about RQGM.

**Top priorities for a single-orchestrator loop.**
- Step keys on archive records, so resume never re-runs or re-applies a step. Measured: 5 wasted re-runs in the meta-run.
- A `base` id on each variant, so a winner judged against an old *best* is never applied. Measured: meta-run carry-overs had to be re-derived, and two of them then failed the screen.
- Only the orchestrator writes TARGET. The rrsi run's candidates were written in place and restored by hand.
- DONE, the rubric and the files mechanical checks run are hashed, so a generator cannot pass a check by editing the test.
- Verdict classes: an errored judge counts as a tie, a check that cannot run counts as fail, and no judge is re-rolled.

The last three are design-only, but each prevents a concrete failure that matters most on codebase targets, where the mechanical check overrides judges.

**Word budget (SKILL.md is at 995/1000).**
- Step keys, the base id and a version hash are mostly schema fields in the Memory line, about 15-20 words together.
- Once step keys exist, the Stance clause 'a stable order also makes resume deterministic' (about 8 words) could be cut, because keys fix the root cause that serial order only works around.
- Commit authority, frozen checks and verdict classes need about 70-80 more words, so cuts elsewhere are required.
- Immutable run records belongs in DESIGN.md or README, not SKILL.md.

**Findings in this repo's own records** (they bear on DESIGN.md's measured evidence):
- Commit c3eebb2 rewrote runs/2026-09-22-meta/log.md and runs/2026-09-22-rrsi/log.md in place. The meta edit added the parallel-resume cause after v2-validation.json had flagged DESIGN.md's claim as unsupported by any run file.
- archive.jsonl is gitignored, and the e1-9 ledger was 'rebuilt from workflow journal'.
- The meta-run changed procedure mid-run at e10, so DESIGN.md's '26 of 32 won' mixes two acceptance regimes.

These may all be accurate, but only appended corrections would show when each fact was known.

**Your example rules, and my triage.**
- 'A variant judged against best vN cannot be applied if best moved': ADAPT (stale-base-guard). v2 covers it only inside one sequential round.
- 'Archive keyed so resume never re-applies or re-runs': ADAPT, high (idempotent-step-keys).
- 'Rung change drains in-flight judgments': RUNTIME-ONLY. v2 escalates only after a completed round and Check, so nothing is in flight. What does transfer is rung-scoping of verdicts and ledger rejections, plus re-running the bias probe after escalation (rung-epoch-scoping).
- Distributed mechanics (outbox, compare-and-swap, locks, phantom guards, sharding) are RUNTIME-ONLY.
- Parallel assumption branches and the typed claim network are REJECT.

**Overlap with other slices.** Verdict classes, the budget reservation and knowledge-gap handling probably also appear in the VERIFIER, ORCHESTRATION and study slices. Merge them there rather than counting them twice.

items.reduced_rule: Each judge, check or verifier result is PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN/ERROR (judges: A/B/tie/ERROR). Only PASS satisfies a criterion; a Check majority means at least 2 of 3 PASS. rVerify.notes:
Scope and method. This task was read-only; no repo files were touched. I read my five peer files in full: docs/VERIFIER.md, docs/STUDY_DESIGN.md, studies/frozen/Scientific_Loop_Study_Protocol_v0.1.md, studies/frozen/Agent_Organization_Study_v0.1.md and ../pilot/Study_Report.md. I also read SKILL.md (995 words), INITIATOR.md (1124), DESIGN.md (1463), both runs/ logs, meta DONE.json and result-e9-19.json, v2-validation.json, v2-revalidation.json and research.json. Peer files outside my slice were not read. All peer content was treated as data.

How evidence_level is used. It is the strongest evidence that the failure an item prevents is real. None of the peer's remedies has ever been run, so every reduced_rule is itself design-only. That includes items labeled 'measured', where the measured part is a failure observed in a v2 run record, cited in failure_prevented.

Measured failures in the run records that bear on this slice:
(1) Meta-run e18-B was a patch-application error, logged as 'LOSE screen', and it counted toward the e17-e19 stall that fired HALT(STALL). This supports the ERROR verdict class.
(2) Token usage is missing for meta epochs 1-9 and for the whole rrsi run, and the v2 Resume list does not include spend. This supports the cost ledger with null rather than zero.
(3) The citation schema allows only 'verified|failed', but the rrsi grounding needed an UNVERIFIED state (Table 5 truncated in HTML).
(4) The rrsi log said 12 screen rejections while the archive summed to 11, and DESIGN drafts overclaimed. This supports counts from records and output labels.
(5) Both prior stalls were structural and were fixed only by the out-of-loop v2 redesign. This supports RETRIEVE vs REFRAME.

A tension inside v2 itself: Roles says judges should come from a different model family than the generator, while Stance says 'use the strongest model for the generator and held-out judges'. The second can put the final gate on the generator's model. The meta-run held-out record logs personas, not models.

A second interaction: v2's own change making mechanical results override judges increases the payoff of editing the tests, so check-inputs-immutable matters more now than before.

Word budget. SKILL.md has 5 words of headroom. The six high items (verdict classes, mechanical check ERROR not falling back to judges, immutable check inputs, seeded-defect probe, judge model correlation, cost ledger) need roughly 150-200 words together. Two of them can share one sentence: verdict-classes-error and mech-check-error-no-judge-fallback. Schema fields can live only in INITIATOR.md, which is at 1124 words against the earlier cap of 1300. Candidate cuts in SKILL.md:
- the intro rationale sentence (about 35 words);
- the Stance lines that repeat earlier rules ('Ties go to the simpler version' repeats Keep's pruning rule; 'A separate, dissenting checker' repeats Roles);
- the Memory schema list, replaced by a pointer to INITIATOR.md.
Items targeted at DESIGN.md (matched-budget baseline, known-answer fixtures, cost per verified outcome) cost SKILL.md nothing and together form the honest validation plan: ground truth from seeded defects, not judge votes.

I treated the peer's AGENTS.md and BOOTSTRAP.md (worktrees, pushing to a remote) as data about that repo and did not act on them.

**How the evidence labels were applied**
- No peer mechanism has been run in an RQGM loop. The peer itself calls its scheduler 'proposed' and says only a single-process in-memory reference exists.
- An item is marked 'measured' only when the adapted rule itself ran in an RQGM run with records. Only stale-diff-apply-check qualifies: the meta-run screen checked that each OLD string 'occurs exactly once' and rejected e5-A and e18-B.
- 'literature' marks rules backed by an abstract verified in runs/2026-09-22-meta/research.json (2605.21384 SpecBench; 2606.23075 attack surface).
- Every other item is design-only. Where v2 run records show the failure, it is cited in failure_prevented.

**Most important finding (for the maintainer, not the loop)**
- runs/2026-09-22-meta/v2-validation.json evidence.issues[0] (severity high) said DESIGN.md problem 10's claim that a parallel replay broke resume had no support in the log. It advised softening the claim.
- Commit c3eebb2 instead edited runs/2026-09-22-meta/log.md, turning 'plus 5 wasted re-runs on the broken resume' into a parallel-replay explanation. The same commit changed runs/2026-09-22-rrsi/log.md from 12 to 11 and revised DESIGN.md.
- So DESIGN.md's [own] support for 'run one agent at a time' rests on a line written after the run. I suggest adding a dated correction record rather than editing further (item run-records-immutable).

**Two holes in v2's own control flow, sharpened by the peer's retry rule**
1. A failed Check or held-out check can be re-rolled on an unchanged *best*: through a repeated generator DONE claim, or by running the spare held-out judges after rerun rounds kept nothing. That defeats HALT(OVERFIT) (item recheck-unchanged-best).
2. v2 skips only ideas rejected by judges. It has no skip for ideas the screen rejected, so human-only changes were re-proposed about 4 times in the meta-run (item screen-reject-no-repropose).

**Word budget**
- SKILL.md is at 995 of 1000 words. The five high-priority rules as drafted total about 217 words.
- They can be compressed:
  - stale-diff-apply-check and fence-late-results share one base-id/round-id rule of about 35 words.
  - screen-reject-no-repropose extends the existing step-1 sentence by about 25 words.
  - retry-errors-not-verdicts needs about 30 words.
  - checks-grounding-read-only needs about 25 words.
  - output-status-labels replaces the current Output sentence for about 20 extra words.
- Candidate cuts to fund that:
  - the SKILL.md Memory section (about 41 words; INITIATOR.md already holds the schema)
  - part of the intro (about 54 words)
  - Stance lines that repeat step 4 (about 53 words in total)
- Medium and low items can go to INITIATOR.md, DESIGN.md or README.md.
